--- title: "Likelihood and priors" description: "Name the distribution you think produced the data, and the loss follows: squared error assumes a Normal outcome, Poisson deviance a Poisson one. Add a belief about how large the coefficients are, and the penalty follows too." order: 4 categories: [optimisation] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## Name the distribution and the loss follows [Loss functions](loss-functions.qmd) ended with a table: squared error for a measurement, Poisson deviance for a count, log loss for presence or absence. Those losses are not a list to memorise. Each comes from one principle, **maximum likelihood**: say what kind of distribution you think produced the data, and the loss follows from it. The same principle explains the penalties that [Regularisation](../05-generalisation/regularisation.qmd) adds to a loss: each is a belief, held before the data arrive, about how large the coefficients are likely to be. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Likelihood reads probability backwards Probability starts from a model and asks how likely the data are. **Likelihood** starts from the data and asks which parameter values make them most likely. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mu <- seq(0.05, 15, length.out = 400) one <- tibble(mu, likelihood = dpois(3, mu)) |> ggplot(aes(mu, likelihood)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = ml_palette[["blue"]]) + labs(x = "Expected count μ", y = "P(count = 3)", title = "One station, counted 3") counts <- c(3, 0, 11) joint <- tibble(mu, L = dpois(counts[1], mu) * dpois(counts[2], mu) * dpois(counts[3], mu)) three <- map_dfr(counts, \(k) tibble(mu, L = dpois(k, mu), curve = paste("counted", k))) |> ggplot(aes(mu, L)) + geom_line(aes(group = curve), colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], linewidth = 0.5) + geom_line(data = joint |> mutate(L = L / max(L) * 0.3), colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], linewidth = 1.1) + geom_vline(xintercept = mean(counts), linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]) + labs(x = "Expected count μ", y = "Likelihood", title = "Three stations, and their product") one + three ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![On the left, the Poisson probability of counting exactly 3 animals, for each expected count μ. It peaks at μ = 3. On the right, the same curve for three stations that caught 3, 0 and 11 (grey), and their product (red), rescaled to fit. The product peaks at 4.67, the mean of the three counts, and is narrower than any single curve.](likelihood-and-priors_files/figure-html/fig-one-station-1.png){#fig-one-station fig-alt='Two panels. The left panel shows a single humped curve rising from zero at mu equals zero to a peak of about 0.22 at mu equals 3, then falling slowly towards zero by mu equals 15. The right panel shows three thin grey curves peaking near zero, near 3 and near 11, and a taller narrow red curve peaking at 4.7, marked by a dashed line. The red curve is narrower than every grey curve.' width=1500} ::: ::: ::: Take one station where 3 animals were counted, and suppose the counts follow a Poisson distribution with some expected count $\mu$. If $\mu$ were 3, a count of 3 would be quite likely; if $\mu$ were 0.2 or 30, it would be a surprise. Plotting that probability against $\mu$ gives the likelihood for that station. With one station, almost any $\mu$ between 1 and 8 is plausible. Stations are independent, so the probability of several counts together is the product of their probabilities. The product is high only where one value of $\mu$ explains all the counts at once, so it is narrower than any single curve, and each extra station narrows it further. The **maximum likelihood estimate** is the value at its peak. ## Taking logs turns the likelihood into a loss The survey has 749 stations with chlorophyll and depth measured. The product of 749 probabilities, each below one, is so small that R stores it as 0. Taking the logarithm turns the product into a sum, which a computer handles easily, and does not move the peak. Fitting algorithms find a lowest point, not a highest one, so they minimise the **negative log-likelihood** instead. That is a loss summed over the data, exactly like the objectives on [Loss functions](loss-functions.qmd). Change the distribution, and the loss changes with it. | If the outcome is assumed to be… | The negative log-likelihood is… | Used by | | --- | --- | --- | | Normal, with the same spread everywhere | Squared error | Linear regression | | Laplace, a sharper peak with heavier tails | Absolute error | Least absolute deviations | | Poisson | Poisson deviance | Poisson regression | | Bernoulli, yes or no | Log loss | Logistic regression | ::: {.diagram} ![A distribution for the response gives a loss. A Normal response, a measurement that can take any value with the same spread everywhere, gives squared error. A Poisson response, a count, gives Poisson deviance. A Bernoulli response, presence or absence, gives log loss.](img/distributions-to-losses.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Normal, gives squared error, a measurement that can take any value: a bell curve centred on a dashed line marked prediction, with the part of the curve below a dashed zero line shaded; same spread everywhere, and values below zero allowed. Poisson, gives Poisson deviance, a count of 0, 1, 2 and so on: bars for counts from 0 to 10, highest near 3; whole numbers from zero, with spread growing with the mean. Bernoulli, gives log loss, presence or absence: a short bar for absent and a taller bar for present; one probability of presence, the rest goes to absence. A note says: name the distribution, and its negative log-likelihood is the loss."} ::: The first row matters most. Squared error assumes a Normal outcome with the same spread everywhere, whether or not anyone says so. A Normal distribution runs below zero, and nothing in squared error objects to a negative prediction, which is why [polynomial regression](../03-supervised-learning/linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd) predicted a negative count. Poisson regression names a distribution that stops at zero, and the problem goes away. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The maths, if you want it With $p(y_i \mid \theta)$ the probability of observation $i$ under parameters $\theta$, $$\text{maximise } \sum_i \log p(y_i \mid \theta) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \text{minimise } \sum_i -\log p(y_i \mid \theta)$$ For a Normal outcome with mean $\hat y_i$ and standard deviation $\sigma$, $$-\log p(y_i \mid \hat y_i, \sigma) = \frac{(y_i - \hat y_i)^2}{2\sigma^2} + \log \sigma + \tfrac{1}{2}\log 2\pi$$ For a fixed $\sigma$, only the first term depends on the predictions, and it is squared error divided by a constant, so the same line minimises both. ::: ## A prior becomes a penalty Maximum likelihood looks at nothing but the data. With many stations that is a strength. With a small survey and many inputs, it reports whatever those few stations happen to show, including effects far larger than any the species could have. A **prior** is what you believe about a parameter before seeing the data, written as a distribution: "the effect of one standard deviation of temperature is usually within about ±2 animals" is a prior on the temperature coefficient. **Maximum a posteriori** (MAP) estimation multiplies the likelihood by the prior, a combination called the **posterior**, and takes its highest point. Many stations outweigh a loose prior; a few stations get pulled towards it. Take the negative log of a prior, as the likelihood's was taken above, and it becomes a penalty: a second term added to the loss that grows as the coefficients move away from zero. ::: {.diagram} ![A flat prior gives no penalty, which is maximum likelihood. A Normal prior centred on zero gives the squared penalty of ridge regression, which shrinks every coefficient but sets none to zero. A Laplace prior gives the absolute penalty of the lasso, which can set some coefficients to zero.](img/priors-to-penalties.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Flat prior, gives no penalty, maximum likelihood: a level line across the coefficient axis; a coefficient of 900 is as plausible as one of 0.9. Normal prior, gives the squared penalty, ridge regression: a bell curve centred on zero; most effects small, shrinks every coefficient but zeroes none. Laplace prior, gives the absolute penalty, lasso: a sharp peak at zero; can set some coefficients to zero. A note says: choose a prior on the coefficients, and its negative log is the penalty."} ::: A Normal prior centred on zero gives the sum of the squared coefficients, the penalty of ridge regression, with a weight λ (lambda) equal to the noise variance over the prior's variance: noisy data or a tight prior pull harder. Maximum likelihood is not free of assumptions either: its flat prior treats a coefficient of 900 as just as plausible as one of 0.9. The prior is stated per standard deviation of each input, so the inputs are standardised first, as [Scaling and encoding](../02-marine-data/scaling-and-encoding.qmd) advises for any penalty. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The maths, if you want it MAP maximises the log-likelihood plus the log-prior: $$\hat\beta_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\max_\beta \; \log p(y \mid \beta) + \log p(\beta)$$ With a Normal outcome of standard deviation $\sigma$ and a Normal prior $\beta_j \sim \text{Normal}(0, \tau)$ on each coefficient, this is $$-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i (y_i - x_i^\top\beta)^2 \;-\; \frac{1}{2\tau^2}\sum_j \beta_j^2 + \text{const}$$ Multiply by $-2\sigma^2$, and maximising it becomes minimising $$\sum_i (y_i - x_i^\top\beta)^2 + \lambda \sum_j \beta_j^2, \qquad \lambda = \frac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2}$$ which is the ridge objective. A Laplace prior puts $\lvert\beta_j\rvert$ in place of $\beta_j^2$, which is the lasso. ::: ## Worked example ### Least squares is the Normal likelihood We fit a line of abundance against standardised chlorophyll twice: once by writing down the Normal negative log-likelihood and minimising it with `optim()`, once with `lm()`. The likelihood never mentions a squared residual. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} X <- model.matrix(~ chl_z, data = d) # The spread sigma is a parameter too. It is searched on the log scale, so the # search cannot propose a negative one. neg_log_lik_normal <- function(par) { -sum(dnorm(y, mean = X %*% par[1:2], sd = exp(par[3]), log = TRUE)) } normal_mle <- optim(c(0, 0, 1), neg_log_lik_normal, method = "BFGS", control = list(reltol = 1e-14, maxit = 5000)) ls_fit <- lm(abundance ~ chl_z, data = d) tibble( method = c("Maximum likelihood", "Least squares, lm()"), intercept = c(normal_mle$par[1], coef(ls_fit)[1]), slope = c(normal_mle$par[2], coef(ls_fit)[2]), sigma = c(exp(normal_mle$par[3]), sqrt(mean(residuals(ls_fit)^2))) ) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 4))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|method | intercept| slope| sigma| |:-------------------|---------:|------:|------:| |Maximum likelihood | 4.008| 1.8238| 4.5013| |Least squares, lm() | 4.008| 1.8238| 4.5013|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import statsmodels.api as sm from scipy.optimize import minimize from scipy.stats import norm, poisson from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, PoissonRegressor, Ridge from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() def standardise(column): return (column - column.mean()) / column.std() d = survey[["abundance", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "depth_m"]].dropna() d = d.assign(chl_z=standardise(d["chlorophyll_mg_m3"]), depth_z=standardise(d["depth_m"])) y = d["abundance"].to_numpy() X = sm.add_constant(d[["chl_z"]]).to_numpy() # The spread sigma is a parameter too. It is searched on the log scale, so the # search cannot propose a negative one. def neg_log_lik_normal(par): return -norm.logpdf(y, loc=X @ par[:2], scale=np.exp(par[2])).sum() normal_mle = minimize(neg_log_lik_normal, x0=[0, 0, 1], method="BFGS", options={"gtol": 1e-8}) ls_fit = LinearRegression().fit(d[["chl_z"]], y) pd.DataFrame({ "method": ["Maximum likelihood", "Least squares, LinearRegression"], "intercept": [normal_mle.x[0], ls_fit.intercept_], "slope": [normal_mle.x[1], ls_fit.coef_[0]], "sigma": [np.exp(normal_mle.x[2]), np.sqrt(np.mean((y - ls_fit.predict(d[["chl_z"]])) ** 2))], }).round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | method | intercept | slope | sigma | |:--------------------------------|------------:|--------:|--------:| | Maximum likelihood | 4.008 | 1.8238 | 4.5013 | | Least squares, LinearRegression | 4.008 | 1.8238 | 4.5013 | ::: ::: ::: The two agree to the fourth decimal place: asking for the line that makes the counts most likely under a Normal distribution gives the least-squares line. ### Poisson regression is the Poisson likelihood Changing `dnorm` to `dpois`, and passing the weighted sum through $e$ so that the expected count stays above zero, gives Poisson regression. We add depth and its square, as in [Regression for counts](../03-supervised-learning/count-regression.qmd). ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Xp <- model.matrix(~ chl_z + depth_z + I(depth_z^2), data = d) neg_log_lik_poisson <- function(b) { -sum(dpois(y, lambda = exp(drop(Xp %*% b)), log = TRUE)) } poisson_mle <- optim(rep(0, ncol(Xp)), neg_log_lik_poisson, method = "BFGS", control = list(reltol = 1e-14, maxit = 5000)) poisson_glm <- glm(abundance ~ chl_z + depth_z + I(depth_z^2), data = d, family = poisson) tibble( term = colnames(Xp), `by optim` = poisson_mle$par, `by glm()` = coef(poisson_glm) ) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 5))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | by optim| by glm()| |:------------|--------:|--------:| |(Intercept) | 1.41315| 1.41315| |chl_z | 0.24063| 0.24063| |depth_z | -0.16657| -0.16657| |I(depth_z^2) | -0.09586| -0.09586|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} Xp = sm.add_constant(d[["chl_z", "depth_z"]].assign(depth_z2=d["depth_z"] ** 2)) def neg_log_lik_poisson(b): return -poisson.logpmf(y, mu=np.exp(Xp.to_numpy() @ b)).sum() poisson_mle = minimize(neg_log_lik_poisson, x0=np.zeros(Xp.shape[1]), method="BFGS", options={"gtol": 1e-8}) poisson_glm = sm.GLM(y, Xp, family=sm.families.Poisson()).fit() # scikit-learn's PoissonRegressor adds a penalty by default (alpha=1.0); # alpha=0 switches it off, and then it fits the same likelihood. poisson_sk = PoissonRegressor(alpha=0, max_iter=1000).fit(Xp.drop(columns="const"), y) pd.DataFrame({ "by minimize": poisson_mle.x, "by statsmodels": poisson_glm.params, "by PoissonRegressor": [poisson_sk.intercept_, *poisson_sk.coef_], }).round(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | | by minimize | by statsmodels | by PoissonRegressor | |:---------|--------------:|-----------------:|----------------------:| | const | 1.41315 | 1.41315 | 1.41314 | | chl_z | 0.24063 | 0.24063 | 0.24063 | | depth_z | -0.16657 | -0.16657 | -0.16656 | | depth_z2 | -0.09586 | -0.09586 | -0.09586 | ::: ::: ::: The coefficients agree to five decimal places. `glm(family = poisson)` is this likelihood with a faster search, and the Python tab shows that scikit-learn's `PoissonRegressor` carries a penalty unless it is switched off. ### A Normal prior gives ridge regression A pilot survey might have forty stations. We draw forty at random and fit abundance on twelve inputs: depth and temperature with their squares, chlorophyll, salinity, and substrate and season as dummy columns. Every input is standardised on the forty stations, so each coefficient is the change in abundance for one standard deviation of its input. We fit three times: by maximum likelihood; by MAP, writing down the Normal likelihood plus a Normal prior with a standard deviation of 1 on every coefficient; and by the ridge formula, with λ equal to the noise variance over the prior variance. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pilot <- survey |> select(abundance, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3, salinity_psu, substrate, season) |> drop_na() X_all <- model.matrix( ~ depth_m + I(depth_m^2) + temperature_c + I(temperature_c^2) + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season, data = pilot )[, -1] # Forty stations, standardised on themselves; abundance is centred on their # mean, so the model needs no intercept. rows <- sample(nrow(pilot), 40) X_train <- scale(X_all[rows, ]) y_train <- pilot$abundance[rows] - mean(pilot$abundance[rows]) sigma <- summary(lm(y_train ~ X_train - 1))$sigma # noise sd, unpenalised fit tau <- 1 # prior sd on each coefficient neg_log_posterior <- function(b) { -sum(dnorm(y_train, X_train %*% b, sigma, log = TRUE)) - sum(dnorm(b, 0, tau, log = TRUE)) } map_fit <- optim(rep(0, ncol(X_train)), neg_log_posterior, method = "BFGS", control = list(reltol = 1e-14, maxit = 10000)) ridge <- function(lambda) { drop(solve(t(X_train) %*% X_train + lambda * diag(ncol(X_train)), t(X_train) %*% y_train)) } lambda <- sigma^2 / tau^2 coefs <- tibble( term = str_replace(colnames(X_train), "^(substrate|season)", "\\1: "), `maximum likelihood` = ridge(0), MAP = map_fit$par, ridge = ridge(lambda) ) coefs |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | maximum likelihood| MAP| ridge| |:------------------|------------------:|------:|------:| |depth_m | 1.018| -0.450| -0.450| |I(depth_m^2) | -1.640| -0.585| -0.585| |temperature_c | 9.234| 0.264| 0.264| |I(temperature_c^2) | -6.778| -0.176| -0.176| |chlorophyll_mg_m3 | -0.205| 0.477| 0.477| |salinity_psu | 0.719| 0.543| 0.543| |substrate: mud | 0.547| 0.487| 0.487| |substrate: rock | -0.888| -0.783| -0.783| |substrate: sand | -0.363| -0.142| -0.142| |season: summer | -3.062| -0.902| -0.902| |season: autumn | -1.291| -0.020| -0.020| |season: winter | -0.249| -0.422| -0.422|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} pilot = survey[["abundance", "depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season"]].dropna().reset_index(drop=True) X_all = pd.concat([ pilot[["depth_m"]], (pilot["depth_m"] ** 2).rename("depth_m^2"), pilot[["temperature_c"]], (pilot["temperature_c"] ** 2).rename("temperature_c^2"), pilot[["chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"]], pd.get_dummies(pilot[["substrate", "season"]], drop_first=True, prefix_sep=": ", dtype=float), ], axis=1) # Forty stations, standardised on themselves; abundance is centred on their # mean, so the model needs no intercept. A different random 40 from R's, so # the numbers differ from the page's. rows = np.random.default_rng(2026).choice(len(pilot), size=40, replace=False) X_train = standardise(X_all.iloc[rows]) y_train = pilot["abundance"].iloc[rows] - pilot["abundance"].iloc[rows].mean() sigma = np.sqrt(sm.OLS(y_train, X_train).fit().scale) # noise sd, unpenalised fit tau = 1 # prior sd on each coefficient def neg_log_posterior(b): return (-norm.logpdf(y_train, X_train.to_numpy() @ b, sigma).sum() - norm.logpdf(b, 0, tau).sum()) map_fit = minimize(neg_log_posterior, np.zeros(X_train.shape[1]), method="BFGS", options={"gtol": 1e-10}) def ridge(lam): return np.linalg.solve(X_train.T @ X_train + lam * np.eye(X_train.shape[1]), X_train.T @ y_train) lam = sigma**2 / tau**2 # scikit-learn's Ridge makes the same objective smallest, with alpha in the # place of lambda. sk_ridge = Ridge(alpha=lam, fit_intercept=False).fit(X_train, y_train) pd.DataFrame({ "term": X_train.columns, "maximum likelihood": ridge(0), "MAP": map_fit.x, "ridge": ridge(lam), "Ridge()": sk_ridge.coef_, }).round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | term | maximum likelihood | MAP | ridge | Ridge() | |:------------------|---------------------:|-------:|--------:|----------:| | depth_m | -10.9 | -0.685 | -0.685 | -0.685 | | depth_m^2 | 9.354 | 0.02 | 0.02 | 0.02 | | temperature_c | 10.85 | 0.061 | 0.061 | 0.061 | | temperature_c^2 | -10.718 | -0.47 | -0.47 | -0.47 | | chlorophyll_mg_m3 | 1.444 | 1.024 | 1.024 | 1.024 | | salinity_psu | 0.667 | 0.016 | 0.016 | 0.016 | | substrate: mud | 1.605 | 0.797 | 0.797 | 0.797 | | substrate: gravel | 1.264 | 0.46 | 0.46 | 0.46 | | substrate: rock | -1.932 | -0.58 | -0.58 | -0.58 | | season: summer | -1.184 | -0.387 | -0.387 | -0.387 | | season: autumn | -0.674 | -0.195 | -0.195 | -0.195 | | season: winter | 0.658 | -0.426 | -0.426 | -0.426 | ::: ::: ::: The MAP and ridge columns agree to 7 decimal places: the same answer reached from two directions, with λ = 15.7. Setting λ to zero gives back maximum likelihood, the first column. There, temperature and its square, two closely related columns, take large opposite values that partly cancel, 9.23 and −6.78 animals per standard deviation. That is what twelve inputs on forty stations allow. The prior pulls them to 0.26 and −0.18. [Regularisation](../05-generalisation/regularisation.qmd) tests whether such shrinking predicts new stations better, and chooses λ on held-out data. ## Forests and boosting have no likelihood A random forest or a boosted model makes a loss small, usually squared error, but states no distribution for the outcome, so it has no likelihood to compare and no prior to state. The flexible methods of [Choosing a method](../03-supervised-learning/choosing-a-method.qmd) give up these tools in exchange for fitting any shape. A penalty can also stop being a prior. Once λ is chosen from the data, as [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd) does, it is no longer a belief held before the survey, so report it as a tuned setting. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - **Likelihood** is the probability of the data at given parameter values; the **maximum likelihood estimate** is the value that makes the data most likely. - Its negative log is a loss. Name the distribution, and the loss follows: Normal gives squared error, Poisson gives Poisson deviance, Bernoulli gives log loss. Written by hand, these reproduced `lm()` and `glm()`. - Squared error assumes a Normal outcome, which is why it allows negative counts. - A **prior**'s negative log is a penalty: a Normal prior gives ridge regression, a Laplace prior the lasso, and a flat prior maximum likelihood. Here MAP and ridge agreed to 7 decimal places. - Forests and boosting state no distribution, and a λ chosen on the data is a tuned setting, not a prior. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. The negative log-likelihood of a Laplace distribution with spread $s$ is `sum(abs(y - mu)) / s + length(y) * log(2 * s)`. Fit a line of abundance against `chlorophyll_mg_m3` by minimising it with `optim()`, and compare the intercept and slope with the absolute-error line on [Loss functions](loss-functions.qmd). 2. Double `sigma` and refit, leaving `tau` alone. Predict first which way the coefficients move, then check against λ = σ²/τ². 3. Replace the Normal prior in `neg_log_posterior()` with a Laplace one, `sum(abs(b)) / tau` in place of the `dnorm()` term, and refit. Do any coefficients reach exactly zero?
